title: Principal Component Analysis
one_sentence_summary: PCA finds orthogonal directions that preserve as much variation in the data as possible.
quick_recall: Center the data, find its high-variance directions, and project onto the leading ones. The leading principal components compress correlated structure, not necessarily task-relevant information.
big_picture: PCA is a change of coordinates: instead of describing data along the original features, it describes it along directions the dataset itself varies most.
intuition: A long, thin cloud can be summarized well by its long axis. PCA finds that axis, then the next best perpendicular axis, and so on. Keeping only the first axes removes directions with relatively little observed variation.
core_explanation: After centering, PCA forms a covariance matrix and finds its eigenvectors. Each eigenvector is a direction; its eigenvalue gives the variance along that direction. Sorting by eigenvalue lets us retain a lower-dimensional projection that preserves the most variance under PCA's linear, squared-error view of reconstruction.
why_it_matters: PCA can reduce noise and dimensionality before visualization, density estimation, or a Gaussian Mixture Model. It can also discard small but predictive variation, so validation still matters.

mathematical_foundation.overview: Centering, covariance, and the principal directions

sections.title: Center before measuring directions
sections.explanation: Centering puts the data cloud around the origin. Without it, the second-moment calculation can mistake a nonzero mean for variation around the mean.

equations.explanation: X is the data matrix and mu is the feature-wise mean. X_c contains each observation's deviation from its typical value, which is the variation PCA intends to describe.

sections.title: Covariance and principal axes
sections.explanation: The covariance matrix encodes spread and co-movement. Its eigenvectors are the directions that make projected variance extremal; eigenvalues quantify that variance.

equations.explanation: n is the number of observations. Sigma has one row and column per feature; diagonal entries are variances and off-diagonal entries are covariances.
v_i is a principal direction and lambda_i is the variance of the centered data along it. Keeping the largest lambdas preserves the most observed variation among projections of that size.

common_misconceptions: Maximum variance is not automatically maximum predictive value.
PCA should be fitted on training data only, then applied to validation and test data.
